substitutes: No exercise ball? A large playground ball or a big laundry basket on its side works for Level 1.
title: The Giant Ball Soccer Club
clue: The object is larger than the dog, so grabbing is off the table.
reveal: A big exercise ball cannot be picked up, carried or hugged. It can be nudged, bumped and steered. Your dog works out how to move it, then how to move it where you want. Every level is a small puzzle with a goal, and the goal is a gap between two chairs.
objective: Let your dog discover how to push a large ball, then steer it through a goal over four levels, ending on a mat.
instructions: Set up in a clear room, hallway, driveway or fenced yard with grippy footing. You need a ball too big to pick up (an exercise ball or large playground ball, firm but not rock hard), two chairs or laundry baskets for a goal about four feet apart, a mat and water.
Level 1, discovery: roll the ball out and sit. Say 'yes' and give a treat for any look, sniff or nose touch. Nothing else. If your dog backs off, roll it closer, or just sit near it.
Level 2, push: pay only for touches that make the ball move. Then two moves in a row. Rounds last two minutes. Take a thirty second break every round: ball down, water, no demands.
Level 3, steer: stand on the goal side of the ball. Pay every push that sends it toward you. Move left or right a step so your dog has to push it a different way.
Level 4, goal: stand behind the goal. Pay when the ball crosses the gap. Then move the ball and your dog to a new start spot and run it again.
Hard stop: if your dog starts biting the ball, nipping at your heels or sleeves, or barking at it, stop. Roll the ball out of sight, walk away and settle. Five rounds is the day.
Final whistle: put the ball away, send your dog to the mat and give a quiet post-game press conference about their performance in a low voice. Water and a rest.
twist: The ball is too big to carry, so the only way to win is to work it out with nose, chest and paws, and the goal is whatever gap you choose.
variations: Easier: a smaller ball and one level only. A nose touch that moves it counts as a goal.
No-yard, small-space version: run it in a hallway with a yoga ball against a wall as your backboard.
Outdoor version: a fenced yard, or a driveway or court only when it is quiet and empty, same four levels.
Harder: set two balls and a goal and ask your dog to push only the one you have marked with a towel.
completion: It counts after a push that moves the ball, or after your dog walks off and you put the ball away. A nose touch is a full game.
photoIdea: Your dog mid-push with the big ball in front of their chest, shot at floor level. A blur is fine.
memoryPrompt: What was the first thing your dog did when the ball appeared, and how did they eventually solve it?
supplies: A ball too big for your dog to pick up
dietNotes: Tiny treats from the daily ration. Check labels for xylitol; ask your vet about diet limits.
safety: An exercise ball can pop on claws or teeth. Check it for punctures, and take it away the moment it starts to deflate.
Nipping at the ball, your heels or your sleeves is the stop sign. End the game and give them a quiet reset.
Use grippy footing and keep chairs from tipping.
